title: ULA's Vulcan Rocket Fails Minutes After Liftoff, Destroying 40 Amazon Internet Satellites
excerpt: A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed about 10 minutes after liftoff on Sunday, Nov. 15, destroying its payload of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — the first outright mission failure in ULA's 20-year history.
content:
A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed about 10 minutes after liftoff on Sunday, Nov. 15, destroying its payload of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — the first outright mission failure in ULA's 20-year history.

The 214-foot rocket lifted off from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida at 12:40 p.m. ET, carrying the first batch of Amazon's Leo satellites ever flown on a Vulcan. The six solid rocket boosters and two methane-burning BE-4 engines performed normally, but the anomaly struck during the Centaur upper stage's burn, and the rocket failed to deliver the mission to orbit.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in a statement about 50 minutes after liftoff.

It was Vulcan's fifth flight since its 2024 debut and its first in nine months, after earlier flights were marred by solid rocket booster nozzle problems. It was also the first of 38 Vulcan launches Amazon has purchased to build out Leo, its planned rival to SpaceX's Starlink. ULA says it does not yet have specific data on what went wrong and will work with Amazon and others to find the cause.

The setback matters for the race to connect the country from space. Amazon has about 398 Leo satellites in orbit across 14 launches — roughly 12 percent of the 3,232 it needs for global service — and federal rules require half of the constellation, 1,616 satellites, in orbit by July 2028. Amazon's next Leo launch, an Ariane 6 carrying 36 satellites, is targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has offered the space agency's help with the investigation.

For Webb County, the stakes are indirect but real: satellite internet is one of the few options for homes and ranches beyond the reach of wired broadband, and how fast Amazon can build its constellation — and how reliably — will shape what choices those households have.
